title: El Niño and food inflation in  Sri Lanka: What history tells us | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:28
-     - 88

El Niño 2026/27: Outlook for Sri Lanka

The Department of Meteorology’s outlook1 indicates that El Niño may persist into early 2027 and peak towards the end of 2026. Above-normal rainfall is possible during November–December 2026, followed by a greater risk of drier conditions and higher temperatures between February and April 2027. On this background, this article examines three strong historical El Niño episodes identified by the Department of Meteorology using the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI):2 1982/83, 1997/98 and 2015/16.

Rainfall before drought: An important part of the story

An important feature observed across the three historical El Niño episodes is that the drought conditions, which were generally identified during Jan–Apr, were preceded by relatively heavy rainfall during Oct–Dec of the preceding year. This highlights the importance of examining rainfall patterns not only during drought periods but also in the months leading up to them. This observation is consistent with Sri Lanka’s seasonal rainfall pattern. On a national average,3

rainfall is generally higher during Sep-Dec than during Jan-Apr and Mean temperatures also tend to be relatively high during Mar–May. These seasonal patterns provide important context for understanding the potential effects of El Niño.

During the identified drought months, country-average rainfall was 91% below normal in February 1983, 70% below normal in March 1998 and 51% below normal in April 2016. While the extent of rainfall deficits varied across the three episodes, understanding their potential implications for food prices requires examining not only the drought periods themselves, but also the rainfall conditions in the preceding months. Excessive rainfall during these months can also damage crops and create post-harvest losses as well as transportation and distribution losses, potentially adding to food-price pressures.

When did inflation respond?

Month-on-month (m-o-m) inflation is examined to identify short-term price movements around periods of rainfall deficiencies and assess how quickly these movements may be reflected in consumer prices.

In each episode, the highest m-o-m inflation within the period examined occurred one to two months after the month with the largest rainfall deficit. In 1982/83, m-o-m inflation reached 3.76% in March 1983, following the February largest rainfall deficit. In 1997/98, it reached 3.22% in May, following the March largest deficit. In 2015/16, it reached 1.80% in May, following the April largest rainfall deficit. M-o-m inflation also remained relatively elevated during the following three months after the drought, with average m-o-m inflation rates across the episodes ranging from about 1.3% to 1.6%.

The timing suggests a possible delay between rainfall deficits and price increases, but does not prove a direct causal link. Inflation is also affected by demand, fuel and other commodity prices, exchange rates, seasonal factors and wider economic conditions. Comparisons are further limited because the CCPI series use different base years and consumption baskets. Historical patterns therefore indicate a potential risk, not a definite prediction for 2026/27. The historical comparison is most useful for identifying timing and possible pressure points, rather than predicting a particular inflation rate.

Headline inflation covers a broad range of goods and services; food inflation focuses on food prices. Looking at food inflation separately helps show how food prices moved around periods of rainfall deficiency.

Food prices at the centre of the response

Graph 03: CCPI-based food and non-food inflation (m-o-m) during the 1997/98 and 2015/16 episodes.

Note: The vertical line marks the peak drought month. Source: Department of Census and Statistics

The food and non-food m-o-m inflation series for 1997/98 and 2015/16 suggest that food prices accounted for much of the increase following the identified peak drought months. Over the next three months, average m-o-m food inflation was 2.17% in 1998 and 1.57% in 2016, giving a combined average of 1.87% for the two episodes.

The magnitude of price increases differed between the two episodes. The impact on food prices would have depended on several factors, including the crops affected, the timing and duration of supply disruptions, and the availability of market stocks.

How did selected food prices respond to the 2015/16 El Niño episode?

The movements in selected food subgroups in the Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI) during the 2015/16 El Niño episode provide further insights into food-price developments during this period.

Some of the graphs illustrate changes in the cost of fixed baskets of selected food subgroups, reflecting overall price movements within each group rather than changes in individual food items.

These movements may also have been influenced by other weather conditions and economic factors prevailing at the time. Accordingly, the analysis highlights possible food-price responses associated with the 2015/16 El Niño episode, rather than establishing a direct causal relationship.

Graph 4: Potentially Quicker Price Responses: Vegetables, Fish and Meat.

*Note: Expenditure values represent the estimated cost of the respective consumer baskets based on CCPI weights. These are not displayed, as the analysis focuses on price trends and relative movements over time.

Vegetable prices appear to have been affected by both rainfall and drought conditions. Increases following heavy rainfall were particularly pronounced in up-country vegetables, while low-country and leafy vegetables showed more noticeable increases following the dry spell.  A similar pattern was observed in January 2015, when prices of both low- and up-country vegetables surged following the heavy rainfall in December 2014.

The increases observed from May to July 2016 were also larger or more persistent than those in the corresponding months of 2015 and 2017, suggesting that seasonal influences alone may not fully explain the price movements.

Fish prices recorded notable increases following the dry spell, with the movements being more pronounced in small fish than in large fish during the first three months after the identified drought period. This may
partly reflect changes in marine environmental conditions associated with El Niño, which could affect fish availability. A recent bulletin issued by the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) indicates that El Niño-related warming in the Indian Ocean could place marine ecosystems under thermal stress, potentially affecting the distribution and recruitment of small pelagic species, particularly sardines and mackerel, and thereby influencing catches.

Although prices of both small and large fish typically show seasonal movements between May and July, the magnitude and pace of the increases observed in 2016 were noteworthy compared with the corresponding periods in 2015 and 2017.

Meat prices also increased during the post-drought period, potentially reflecting a shift in demand towards meat as an alternative to fish. Particularly noteworthy was the sharp increase between June and July 2016, which was considerably higher than the movements observed during the corresponding months of 2015 and 2017. Higher animal feed costs and shortages of water may also have

contributed by raising livestock production costs.

Graph 5: Potentially Delayed Price Responses: Rice, Coconut and Fresh Fruits

The response also differed across commodities, with some taking longer to reflect weather-related pressures. Rice prices recorded a more noticeable increase from October 2016, suggesting a possible delayed response to the dry spell. The Maha season may have been relatively less affected due to water availability, while the subsequent Yala cultivation could have faced greater challenges from drought conditions. Any delays in sowing and planting may also have affected the timing of harvesting and market supplies, contributing to the later increase in rice prices. However, these remain possible explanations, as the price data alone do not establish whether Yala cultivation was affected or whether farmers delayed planting. Production cycles, harvesting schedules, existing stocks, storage and the availability of supplies may all influence how quickly weather-related disruptions are reflected in consumer prices.

Coconut prices showed an overall upward trend from December 2016 onwards, despite marginal setbacks during some months. This sustained increase, particularly during 2017, may reflect delayed effects of El Niño-related weather conditions or rainfall patterns preceding the event. Research on Sri Lanka’s coconut sector also suggests that adverse weather conditions may affect coconut supply with a considerable time lag of around ten months to a year (Silva & Matsui, 2026).

Fresh fruit prices also recorded a considerable increase during the 2016 drought period. Notably, the magnitude of this increase was greater than the movements observed during the corresponding period in 2015 and 2017. This suggests that, beyond normal seasonal fluctuations, the dry conditions may have contributed to the price pressures observed in fresh fruits during this period.

Source: Department of Census and Statistics

Taken together, the subgroup evidence points to three important features of the 2015/16 episode: price increases in several vegetable and fish categories emerged after the dry spell had persisted for several months; the timing and magnitude of the movements varied across commodities; and some categories, notably rice and coconuts, recorded more noticeable increases later. Overall, the timing and magnitude of price movements differed across the selected food subgroups. These differences may reflect crop cycles, harvesting patterns, seasonal availability, storage, transport and other supply-side developments. While the observed movements provide useful insights into food-price developments during the 2015/16 episode, they do not independently establish the extent to which El Niño-related weather conditions contributed to the changes.

Lessons from history and the inflation outlook

The historical evidence highlights that food-price developments may be influenced not only by drought conditions but also by rainfall patterns in the preceding months. Food prices accounted for a significant part of the inflation response, although the timing and magnitude of the increases varied across commodities. These historical patterns highlight potential pressure points but do not imply that inflation will follow the same path during the 2026/27 episode.

Sri Lanka’s economic environment has also changed. Expenditure values are estimated to be around three times higher than in 2015/16, this does not necessarily indicate greater household purchasing power, as constrained budgets may limit households’ ability to absorb further price increases.

Monitoring rainfall forecasts alongside crop conditions, vegetable arrivals, fish landings and wholesale and retail prices can help identify food-supply pressures early. History offers lessons about possible risks, not a definitive prediction for 2026/27. The outcome will depend on the severity and duration of weather disruptions and on wider economic conditions and policy responses.

These weather-related risks are emerging at a time when headline inflation has already moved above the 5% inflation target due to several supply-side pressures, including adjustments to energy prices reflecting changes in international fuel prices, partly influenced by geopolitical conflicts, as well as other domestic and external cost pressures.

Sri Lanka reaffirmed its 5% headline inflation target for the next three years in October 2026. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka has also reiterated its commitment to price stability through its Monetary Policy Reviews, emphasising its readiness to take timely and appropriate measures to stabilise inflation around the target while supporting economic activity over the medium term.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in his personal capacity and do not necessarily reflect the views or official position of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. The analysis is intended for informational and discussion purposes and should not be interpreted as an official forecast or policy statement of the Central Bank.

(The author is a Senior Assistant Director, Statistics Department, Central Bank of Sri Lanka)

1. Asia Pacific Alliance for Disaster Management (APAD). (2026). El Niño 2026/27 Weather Outlook Update 001, 12 October 2026.

2. In February 2026, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Climate Prediction Center adopted RONI as its operational index for monitoring and classifying El Niño and La Niña.

3. Source: World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal, Sri Lanka – Historical Climate Data (1991–2020 climatology), based on Climatic Research Unit (CRU) observations.

title: Budget 2027: Lacklustre Budget for decisive year | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:27
-     - 51

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

That 2027 is an important year cannot be disputed. Sri Lanka graduates from the IMF EFF program, having completed many of its commitments on the fiscal front. This Budget was a test of the country’s commitments to its new public financial guardrails. On that front, the Government has done well. There were no major tax concessions granted, although there was a lot of public pressure for it. 

My assessment of Budget 2026 was that it was cautious where needed, but not bold enough where it could be. On Budget 2027, my assessment is that the Government’s cautiousness continues while its sense of boldness seems to have vanished altogether.

Things that are going right: Taxes, investment and digitalisation and trade

While there was much talk about personal income tax relief and VAT relief at many political gatherings in the run up to the Budget, the Government only conceded a little. Raising the personal income tax threshold to Rs. 1.95 million per year and tweaking the tax bands. Books and printed materials have been exempted from VAT, but that is unlikely to cause a major dent in Government revenues. There was no reduction in the rate nor changes to the threshold. 

Proponents of a VAT rate reduction pointed towards cost-of-living relief, but does reducing VAT lead to a reduction in the cost of living? Reducing VAT did not lead to a reduction in the cost of living in December 2019, when rates were almost cut in half. In fact, food prices even rose by 6.3%. More recently, exempting local dairy from VAT did not lead to the expected price drop in April 2025 either. It was a lose-lose situation – the Government lost revenues while consumers continued to pay the same prices. So, reducing VAT for cost-of-living relief is unlikely to have such a desirable outcome.

This Budget appears serious about addressing investment promotion and digitalisation. Many new Bills, amendments, agencies and funding have been pledged for achieving these. Given the level of private sector involvement and interest in these two areas, they may prove to be some of the more successful endeavours of this Government. Land is a major barrier to investment in Sri Lanka – and this Budget takes aim at resolving these too with a Rs. 800 million allocation for the Bimsaviya program and Rs. 140 million for the registration of land titles, digitalisation of land records and the modernisation of land information systems.

Not so right: Para-tariffs and trade agreements

Last year, the Government announced the implementation of the National Tariff Policy. While I raised a concern about the fact that the Government’s revenue numbers at the time didn’t reflect this, this issue seems to have been rectified now. Revenues from para-tariffs like Ports and Airports Development Levy and Cess are indeed phasing out. However, surreptitiously, the revenues from the Special Commodity Levy (SCL) are rising. It is estimated to generate Rs. 170 billion in 2027, Rs. 187 billion in 2028 and Rs. 204 billion in 2029 – these are higher than what was projected in the 2026 Budget.

The SCL was a tariff brought about in 2007 as a composite levy that would ease administration of Sri Lanka’s then-highly complex import tariff regime. It is currently exclusively levied on food items – dhal, onions, potatoes, sprats, dried fish, dairy, fresh fish, pulses and fruits. 

SCL revenues rising is an incredibly strange twist. With the move towards a simplified 4-band Customs duty, and the phasing out of para-tariffs, SCL is a redundant tariff. The need to ease administration of complex tariffs is addressed by the former. However, it appears that the Government intends to use SCL to make up for the revenues lost from the phasing out of PAL and Cess. This may also placate the local industrialists who have been opposing the para-tariff phase out, by offering them some protection against import competition. 

The imposition of SCL is done by Gazette notice, at the discretion of the Minister of Finance. So SCL may be expanded to cover things beyond food – things that the para-tariff phase out was supposed to help with. On the other hand, if SCL continues to be collected on food items, this is an extra burden to consumers – especially when the cost of living is already unaffordable to many. 

In mid-2026, the Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development announced that they would introduce new import standards among other measures to counterbalance the effects of the phase out. Coupling this with the projected SCL revenues, one could argue that it is essentially a continuation of the para-tariff regime in all but name.

On other aspects related to trade, there was mention of the intention to pursue trade agreements with China and India and even negotiate economic cooperation agreements with Oman and UAE. However, there has been no mention of establishing a dedicated office that can see such negotiations through. Negotiating free trade agreements typically take 1-3 years, but Sri Lanka usually takes much longer – 5 or 6 years. Without an institution dedicated to such a feat, it is unlikely that such an ambitious plan can be executed.

Not at all: SOEs, public sector reforms and poverty

This Budget is suspiciously absent on State-owned enterprise reforms. The much-delayed public commercial business management Bill was referred to in passing, but no mention of when it will be tabled in Parliament. The last year Budget also referred to the Bill and promised to present it to Parliament in the first 6 months of 2026. It has not been done so. It further pledged to restructure 44 and liquidate 13 non-commercial entities. Neither has this been done. 

It appears that Sri Lanka will fall back into malaise with respect to State-owned enterprises. Even the well-known problem child – SriLankan Airlines – was only referred to in passing as a burden on the Treasury, with yet another committee appointed to find solutions.

In a similar vein, public sector reforms too are absent in this Budget. While many new allowances and benefits have been announced for various civil servants, there is no mention of rationalising or right-sizing the public service. In fact, Budget estimates show that the Government spending on salaries and benefits and pensions will keep pace with Government revenue – at around 16% and 10% respectively. There is nothing on reforming the civil pension scheme which will be a huge fiscal burden in time to come.

Budget week happened to coincide with the Department of Census and Statistic’s decision to finally release at least preliminary results from the much-delayed Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2025. The survey results are extremely concerning. From my reading of the numbers, my conclusions are that we may be poorer and more in debt than we think. Inequality has surged, and Sri Lanka’s ‘middle-class’ seem to have vanished. Median household income is Rs. 75,882, and median household expenditure is Rs. 94,057 – a gap that is likely bridged with debt. 

The poorest 40% of Sri Lankans live with an average household income of Rs. 36,564. On the other hand, the official poverty line was Rs. 16,417 per person per month and an average household of 3-4 people would need Rs. 55-65,000 per month to meet their basic needs. This means that at least 40% of Sri Lankan households do not earn sufficiently to be above the poverty line.

Poverty and food insecurity are major prevailing economic issues in the country, but despite this stark reality, the allocations for the Aswesuma program are not growing – in fact it is less than what was estimated for 2026; Rs. 230 billion in 2027, against Rs. 240 billion in 2026. There is limited action on food security, besides a few allocations for improving irrigation and the fisheries sector, and reducing the SCL on sprats and dry fish. These are unlikely to alleviate the cost of living nor increase food security in the near future. 

All in all, this Budget lacks the decisiveness to address the many ills that plague our country; from underperforming State-owned entities to poverty and food insecurity. Although the President spoke a lot about economic, social and structural transformation, this Budget fails to embody it.  What Sri Lanka really needs is a Government that is bold enough to push the envelope – to upset the apple cart. Otherwise, we risk sliding back into our old ways.

(The author is an Economist and Co-Founder/Director of Arutha, an economic research and civic education organisation)

title: Budget 2027: Saint abroad, devil at home | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:26
-     - 33

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake delivering 2027 Budget speech in Parliament

For the people of Sri Lanka, development, as the President invoked at the start of his Budget speech, remains a longstanding but unachieved aspiration. Sadly, the 2027 Budget fails to lay the groundwork for fulfilling that aspiration. Worse than a mere failure, it hoodwinks people, as many past Budgets have done. 

The 2027 Budget is best read not as a fiscal plan for development and wellbeing but as a chant of the IMF mantra: a primary surplus of 2.3%, Budget deficit below 5% and debt sustainability. As this article illustrates, a Government enchanted by the IMF mantra deceives people in three ways. 

First, it declares grand fiscal allocations but under-executes them. Second, it subordinates productive investments and social security to investor requirements. Third, it subjects life-sustaining infrastructure to a neoliberal grip. The result is a Budget that acts as a saint abroad and a devil at home.

Under-execution is new austerity

The Government’s claim that the Budget is transformative gains legitimacy from grand Budget allocations. But numbers on paper are not a reason for optimism. Not spending allocated capital expenditure has become a norm, constituting a strategy of fiscal consolidation and a new form of austerity. 

To begin with the last Budget: the 2026 Budget had allocated Rs. 1,380 billion for capital expenditure. However, according to the Mid-Year Fiscal Position Report 2026 issued by the Treasury, only 16.1% had actually been spent by June 2026. According to the Budget, Economic and Fiscal Position Report issued in November, capital expenditure and net lending had increased to 31.6%, equivalent to Rs. 436 billion. 

In 2025, the corresponding figure was 17.2%. The Mid-Year Fiscal Position Report 2025 attributes the fall in expenditure to “delayed execution of the capital Budget” (p. 12). 

According to the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Sri Lanka has consistently fallen behind in terms of capital expenditure. Between 2022 and 2025, only 3% of GDP was spent, whereas the Budget allocations ranged between 5% and 6% of GDP. Figure 1, extracted from the Asian Development Outlook for Sri Lanka issued in April 2026, proves that under-execution of capital expenditure is a standard practice. 

Figure 1: Under-Execution of Capital Expenditure

Source: ADB Outlook for Sri Lanka, April 2026

The conventional understanding of austerity is living within one’s means or slashing of public expenditure. What the data show is something beyond that: Governments, including the NPP Government, have not spent even the funding allocated. The ADB and IMF analyses of underutilisation of funds point to limitations of the public sector in terms of capabilities, and governance (delays in procurement, land acquisition, feasibility assessment and inter-agency coordination), which could be overcome through more public-private partnerships. These analyses assume that private sector is better endowed with skills and expertise. However, what if under-execution is an outcome of austerity internalised into Government psyche through decades of austerity imposed on Governments by the IMF, ADB and World Bank? 


Cross-country data, particularly for countries under IMF programs, show that under-utilisation of capital funds is a shared practice. According to an early IMF report, Economic Adjustment and Reform in Low-Income Countries (1999), one strategy to contain deficit was to adjust expenditure by cutting capital expenditure. An IMF report in 2026 confirms that cutting capital expenditure is the “residual adjustment tool when fiscal pressures emerge” (IMF, May 13, 2026). The IMF recognises that such fiscal pressures emerge not only from revenue shortfalls but also from delays in external financing. 

As World Bank data on world debt explains, external financing for developing countries has been chronically inadequate. More than being inadequate, external financing has become a major means of capital outflow, thereby working against the developmental aspirations of countries in the global south. The International Debt Report 2026, published by the World Bank, highlights a recurrent pattern that it also identified in previous reports: “Between 2022 and 2025, [Lower-Middle Income Countries] (LMICs) paid about $436.1 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing” (p. xviii). According to the same report, even though low-income countries returned to capital markets in 2025, access came at a greater cost. Except for China, all other low-income countries experienced higher growth rates of debt than of national income. This is the context in which both the IMF and neoliberal lobby groups in Sri Lanka encourage the NPP Government to return to the Bond market. 

Capital under-execution when revenue is not falling, as in Sri Lanka, could hint at dangerous policy moves. Under-investing in capital expenditure while subordinating fiscal policy to the IMF mantra could be interpreted as a purposeful policy to make lending to Sri Lanka attractive to foreign creditors, particularly those in international Bond markets. A primary surplus itself signals positively to creditors indicating that Government has surplus revenue after meeting all non-interest expenses (expenses on salaries, goods, services and capital projects). Under-spending on capital projects, therefore, leaves more money to spend on other things, such as debt servicing. The Government, expecting to return to the international Bond market in the future, is under-spending to enhance its credibility among creditors. 

As Sri Lankans are experiencing firsthand, more borrowing will not by itself deliver development. The very acts of restructuring the economy to please the creditors impose severe constraints on the transformative change that people and the economy need. Apart from imposing undemocratic stabilisation policies, such as raising VAT, reducing employment levels and cutting social security, that ordinary working people in Sri Lanka have had to endure since the default in 2022, purposefully keeping capital investments low so the economy will look better for foreign creditors is almost an act of class warfare against the people who voted the NPP Government to power.

Liberating investors in shackles

Rewarding private investors is as much an overriding theme of the Budget as inspiring foreign creditors. The President’s Budget speech interprets new legal and institutional reforms as a means of “removing shackles that bind our feet from reaching the economic transformation we envisage” (p. 11). In rendering a new meaning to the word “shackles”, historically used in left literature as a rallying cry for working people, the 2027 Budget advocates pro-market reforms to set private investors free from binding State regulations or established communal practices. 


For example, the Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Act 2026 seeks to formalise low-income credit landscape while also eroding the financial commons that low-income people have practised for centuries. As traditional community credit mechanisms are weakened, formalisation will invariably benefit large finance companies with ample opportunity to access financial capital and with the institutional capabilities to respond to regulatory requirements. Other forthcoming Bills, such as the Non-Governmental Organisation (Registration and Supervision) Bill 2026 (not listed in the Budget), also contribute towards formalisation, with the apparent aim of eliminating all forms of informal collective action at community level so that they cease to exist in the future. 

Similarly, the Acts on Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs), and State-Owned Business Enterprises Management Act will carry forward the transfer of public assets and wealth into the hands of the private sector. Forthcoming labour law reforms, specifically eliminating protective clauses on hiring and firing in the Termination of Employment of Workmen Act, which the Chamber of Commerce has been advocating for years, would render workers completely submissive to the whims and fancies of employers.

Compromising resilience

The word “resilience” figures four times in the Budget speech. The repeated emphasis on resilience, by the Government as well as by the IMF, World Bank and ADB, however, is not a positive sign. Rather than recognising the need to invest in and strengthen community infrastructure that enables resilience and helps people preserve life during hard times, both the IFIs and the Government, under the IFI’s spell, approach resilience as a resource pool to be grabbed. 

While this might look like a baseless accusation, comparing Sri Lanka’s trajectory under the IMF with Ghana’s, for example, illustrates how compromising the Sri Lankan Governments have been, and at what cost to ordinary people. Ghana defaulted on its external debt payments in December 2022. Unlike Sri Lanka, Ghana refused to subject pension funds to domestic debt restructuring. Moreover, in 2026, Ghana received a concession from the IMF to lower primary surplus target from 1.5% to 0.5% from 2027 onwards. 

Despite facing acute crises such as Cyclone Ditwah in November 2025 and spillovers from the war against Iran in 2026, the Sri Lankan Government failed to gain flexibility in how IMF targets are achieved, let alone concessions. What we have seen so far is the Government legitimising both the IMF program and the debt restructuring process, making it possible for the IMF to make a comeback as essential and useful mediator in instances of debt crises in the Global South. For the people on whose backs this success story has been written, the future is still bleak. A preliminary report issued by the Department of Census and Statistics on the Household Income and Expenditure Survey 2025 reveals that income inequality between the poorest and richest Sri Lankans has deepened. The poorest 20% earn an average income of Rs. 22,612 while the richest 20% earn Rs. 335,679 per month. The Budget 2027 lowered income tax that the richest 20% are likely to pay, while the poorest 20% received only marginal tax benefits. 


Instead of expanding investment in social security programs, the Government is introducing new loan schemes, akin to 2018 Enterprise Sri Lanka Budget that substituted loans for welfare. New concessional loan programs directed at micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), women-headed households and entrepreneurs employing Aswasuma beneficiaries are meant to spur the growth potential of the rural sector. How can we reconcile introduction of new loan programs in an environment in which household debt is already alarming? 

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) in its Financial Stability Review 2026 cautions about household debt, illustrating how an increase in pawning in the first quarter of 2026 could indicate financial stress at the household level. Figure 2, taken from the CBSL report, illustrates how household consumption loans expanded. In 2026, pawning accounts for the largest source of household consumption loans.

Figure 2: Credit to Consumption

In considering household behaviour vis-à-vis debt, women pawn their gold in times of extreme hardship. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, when lockdown regulations were relaxed, long queues in front of pawning shops were a common sight. Even though the CBSL rationalises the increase in pawning as driven by rising gold prices, pawning as a last-resort option when they urgently need cash, better explains the pawning behaviour of Sri Lankan women. The household debt crisis, particularly among low-income households affected by microfinance, remains unresolved despite women’s protests and election promises, and it is deeply rooted. The increase in pawning shown in Figure 2 could be an indicator of deep indebtedness, not an indicator of any particular capitalising behaviour of people, as the CBSL believes.

Saint abroad, devil at home

What households in Sri Lanka need is not more debt but more enabling investment, in MSMEs, agriculture and fisheries sectors, to break the decades-long funding crisis and financial grip of both money lenders and the formal banks and finance companies. As a people striving to emerge from default, we need more public investment in education, health care, social security and livelihoods to ensure that no one is left behind. Yet, as World Bank human development indicators illustrate, the indicators that matter to ordinary people still lag behind pre-crisis levels. 

Governments have chased macroeconomic stability indicators in a quest to stage a recovery attractive to foreign creditors and investors. The result is a Budget that presents Sri Lanka as a saint abroad while acting as a devil at home: under-executing capital investment, inundating productive sectors and households with more debt, and eroding the very community resilience that has helped people survive hard times. This promises not recovery but deepening crises.

(The author (PhD, Hawai‘i) is a feminist political economist, a senior researcher at the Bandaranaike Centre for International Studies, and a member of the Movement for Climate and Economic Justice (MCEJ) and Yukthi Collective)

title: Beyond the cheque: What Sri Lanka’s children need from business | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:25
-     - 45

Earlier this year, I visited a temporary learning facility for children whose school had been relocated from their hill country estate after Cyclone Ditwah. What struck me was not only what they had lost, but what they were seeing for the first time. Instead of a short walk from their row house to school, the children now take a tuk-tuk down the hill into town. It is no exaggeration to say that their world view was being transformed by this experience. It reminded me that children’s futures are shaped by the opportunities in front of them – and that too often, where a child is born still decides what those opportunities are.

Today is World Children’s Day, and it is worth remembering how far Sri Lanka has already come in widening those opportunities. In 1990, about 23 of every 1,000 children died before their fifth birthday. Today the figure is under six, thanks to free healthcare, a remarkable network of public health midwives and decades of steady public investment.

But recent years have shown how quickly gains can slip. According to the World Bank, poverty more than doubled after 2019, from 11.3% to 24.5% in 2025. Cyclone Ditwah affected more than 275,000 children last year, and the 2025 National Nutrition Month found that almost half of children under five had at least one growth-related problem. The burden falls hardest on children on the plantations, in disaster-hit districts and children with disabilities – those already furthest from opportunity.

Every one of these children has the right to grow, learn and be safe – not someday, but now. Government cannot close these gaps alone, and neither can UNICEF. Children in Sri Lanka need business too.

And there is a window right now that will not stay open for long. Sri Lanka is reforming its education system, including a new early childhood curriculum. The first five years are when a child’s brain develops fastest and when every rupee goes furthest. Getting early learning right – trained teachers, quality preschools, children who arrive at school ready and excited to learn – may be the most important investment the country can make in its next generation. The reform is the chance to build that into the system, rather than fund around it.

The good news is that care for children runs deep in Sri Lanka. The country made education free in 1945, long before most of its neighbours, and has kept it free ever since. WHO and UNICEF data show that almost every Sri Lankan baby receives their routine vaccines in the first year of life. And when Cyclone Ditwah struck, UN figures show that nearly two in three displaced people were taken in by host families and communities rather than staying in safety centers – and more than four months later, some 150,000 people were still being hosted. Families opened their homes to other people’s children without being asked.

Sri Lankan businesses share that instinct. During the economic crisis, companies and individuals helped raise funds for children and families, and after Cyclone Ditwah, businesses gave generously to the recovery.

That generosity has mattered, and it will always be needed when disaster strikes. But much of it still goes to one school, one village or one cause close to a company’s heart – valuable but limited to the children it
happens to reach. The bigger opportunity is to work alongside Government to strengthen the systems every child relies on: schools, health services and social protection. When business backs a system rather than a single project, a good idea in one district can become the norm in all 25, and Sri Lanka as a whole benefits.

The early years are the place to start. In Uva and Central provinces, businesses have worked with provincial authorities and UNICEF to improve preschools – funding that strengthens the public system rather than sitting alongside it. With the education reform under way, multi-year commitments like these could help the new early childhood curriculum reach every classroom, not just the fortunate ones.

It continues inside a company’s own walls. Some of the most powerful things a business can do for children sit in its own policies: parental leave beyond the legal minimum, breastfeeding spaces, childcare and flexible hours. On plantations and in apparel factories, where so many parents work, support for workers’ children is good for families and increasingly valued by export markets. Some firms are already leading – one agribusiness has appointed child protection focal points across its estates – and the Children’s Rights and Business Principles offer a practical guide for others ready to follow.

Business also brings what money alone cannot: know-how in logistics, technology, finance and data – exactly what helps services reach the children who are hardest to reach. In Sri Lanka we are exploring private-sector-led models to bring solar power to schools, clinics and water systems – solutions that make commercial sense and change children’s lives.

And what gets measured gets done. A recent UNICEF review, ‘Making Children Count’, looked at 1,399 listed companies across nine Asian markets, including 52 in Sri Lanka. Nearly three in four had made human rights commitments, but only one in 20 named children as stakeholders. Sri Lanka already has sustainability reporting in place for its top 100 listed companies but in 20 of its 26 indicators, what companies reported achieving for children fell at least 50% short of what they pledged, and markets with mandatory reporting scored more than twice as high as those with voluntary or no guidance. Asking them to report on how they respect children’s rights – in the workplace, in their supply chains and in their marketing – would be a low-cost way to make children visible and to turn goodwill into accountability.

This is also sound economics. Every dollar spent on childhood immunisation returns between $20 and $50 or more, and nutrition programs return more than $20. With an ageing population, where each generation of workers will be smaller than the last, Sri Lanka cannot afford for any child to fall behind. And as the country rebuilds after the economic crisis, investors are watching its people as closely as its balance sheet.


Eighty years ago next month, UNICEF was founded to help children recover from war. Sri Lanka’s children face different challenges today, but the question is the same: not whether we can afford to invest in them, but whether we can afford not to. So here is my challenge. By next World Children’s Day, let everyone of Sri Lanka’s top 100 listed companies report on what it is doing for children’s rights – not just what it has promised, but what it has delivered. Those children in their temporary classroom have already glimpsed a bigger world. Let’s make sure it is there waiting for them.

(The author is the UNICEF Representative in Sri Lanka, a role she assumed in August 2025. She has held senior leadership positions with UNICEF in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Mozambique, overseeing programs in complex humanitarian and development contexts, including responses to COVID-19, political unrest and refugee crises. A UK national, she previously worked with the Aga Khan Foundation and Chatham House, and has an academic background in Development Studies and International Relations)

title: A financially unsavvy CEO is like Columbus sailing without a compass | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:22
-     - 62

It is a quiet, disheartening tragedy to watch Chief Executive Officers (CEOs), even at large, powerful organisations, freeze when faced with basic finance and accounting questions. They often retreat behind the reflexive, rehearsed refrain: “I’ll have to check with my Chief Financial Officer (CFO and get back to you.” Whilst it is disturbing to witness such slavish reliance on the CFO to respond to basic queries, it reveals a glaring void in foundational financial literacy where it ought to be. Seeing someone hold absolute strategic authority while lacking a basic grasp of his/her own balance sheet, cash flows, profitability indicators, et cetera, exposes an uncomfortable reality. It is essential that a CEO is in intimate touch with the core of the business. Running a multi-billion-rupee enterprise on pure vibes and financial blindness is not just dismal; it is the gateway to failure.

In the modern corporate arena, the CEO is revered as the captain steering strategy, inspiring talent, and delivering long-term value. Yet across many Sri Lankan corporates, from listed conglomerates to family enterprises, an uncomfortable paradox persists. CEOs, while proficient in marketing, supply chain, and new business development, and sometimes highly effective as leaders, operate with striking vulnerability in finance due to an ultra-dependent relationship with their CFOs. This is not a delegation. It stems from a self-inflicted fundamental knowledge deficit. Many CEOs struggle with the basic mechanics of working capital cycles and cash flow, viewing financial statements as cryptic compliance documents rather than as navigational dashboards. When confronted with concepts like Discounted Cash Flow (DCF), Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), or Return on Invested Capital (ROIC), the response is often quite bewildering. Financial statements are treated as compliance documents to be signed off, rather than first-instance dashboards for strategic decision-making.

This disproportionate reliance on the CFO creates a dangerous organisational dynamic. When a CEO lacks foundational financial literacy, the CFO ceases to be a strategic partner and inadvertently becomes the sole arbiter of corporate viability. Strategic discussions about capital allocation, merger and acquisition valuations, debt structuring, or pricing models risk becoming one-sided. The CEO is left unable to challenge assumptions, stress-test financial projections, or ask the critical, uncomfortable questions that safeguard a business. Decision-making becomes reactive, driven by a blind trust in spreadsheet outputs rather than a deep, intuitive understanding of financial reality.

Consider a financially unsavvy CEO who uncritically accepts CFO’s optimistic projections based on cheap foreign debt financing and projected export growth, and takes reckless, unmitigated risks. Failing to stress-test currency volatility, liquidity crunches, and rising foreign interest rates leaves the company vulnerable to severe financial distress. Had the CEO possessed basic financial literacy regarding capital structure, foreign exchange exposure, and how an appreciating local currency erodes export competitiveness, he/she could have challenged the CFO’s assumptions before committing to disproportionately heavy foreign debt. Rigorous scrutiny would have driven safer strategic alternatives, such as currency hedging or a phased, risk-controlled expansion.

The danger of this prevailing dilemma cannot be overemphasised, particularly in Sri Lanka’s volatile economic environment. In a landscape marked by shifting interest rates, foreign exchange fluctuations, and tight liquidity constraints, financial illiteracy at the helm is an existential risk. Capital allocation errors, such as over-leveraging during economic upturns or misjudging cost structures during downturns, often stem directly from CEOs who cannot read the financial pulse of their own companies. Furthermore, this dynamic exposes organisations to severe governance risks. Without an independent financial lens at the executive level, oversight diminishes, and operational blind spots multiply.

Admittedly, in corporate leadership, the CEO, irrespective of his core expertise, is expected to be an integrator. He is not expected to understand the granular details of finance. Any attempt to do so will be a poor use of CEO bandwidth because it actively hampers strategic focus. There is, however, a fundamental difference between operational level ‘meddling’ and directorial/managerial questioning. Delegating the technical execution of finance and accounting to the CFO is logical and prudent but delegating their comprehension and application solely to the CFO is reckless.

At its core, corporate finance and accounting provide the language for articulating a company’s operational health, market position, and future trajectory. A CEO who lacks fluency in this language risks making decisions based on blind trust rather than data. Conversely, a CEO who understands balance sheets, capital structures, and cost drivers can lead with precision, allocating resources to build long-term value while safeguarding the organisation against systemic risk. A CEO must be able to read the story behind the figures, detect subtle systemic risks before they surface as crises, and ensure that every financial decision directly aligns with long-term strategy. Without this directorial grasp, a CEO is effectively operating blind, completely dependent on the CFO and the finance function without the capacity for meaningful oversight, constructive dissent, or strategic direction. A company cannot be sustainably led by a chief executive who is blind to the intricacies of finance.

Working alongside finance-savvy leaders, such as the late Anderson Mazoka, former CEO of Boart Longyear and Managing Director at Anglo American Corporation Central Africa (Anglo), Susantha Ratnayake, former Chairman/CEO of John Keells Holdings (JKH), and Ajit Gunewardena, former Executive Director of JKH and current Chairman of PickMe, Fintrex, and Teejay, and various CEOs/CFOs in the JKH Group, impressed on me the critical value of executive financial literacy. Their sharp, searching questions kept me on my toes. Having also served as CEO of Anglo following Anderson Mazoka’s resignation to contest Zambia’s presidency, and as Group Finance Director at both Anglo and JKH, I have experienced firsthand the extent of financial literacy a CEO must possess to lead effectively.

Financial statement literacy: Reading the core ledger

A CEO must read the primary financial statements as an interconnected account of operational decisions, not as separate accounting exercises. Together, the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement reveal a company’s assets, liabilities, shareholders’ equity, gearing, profitability, and cash generation. Understanding them helps a CEO assess short-term liquidity and long-term leverage. Overlooking these fundamentals can be fatal. The collapse of Toys “R” Us stands as one of corporate history’s most striking examples of how aggressive financial engineering can extinguish a retail giant. At its peak, the brand commanded immense cultural mindshare and strong seasonal sales, yet structural debt eliminated the strategic flexibility required to survive changing consumer realities. 

While the Balance Sheet is a snapshot of net wealth, the income statement records revenues, operational costs, and net margins over a specified reporting window. A CEO must look past top-line growth to evaluate fixed versus variable overhead and identify margin contraction early. Spotify built its audio platform on this level of scrutiny, balancing heavy content licensing fees and royalty costs against subscriber acquisition and retention to achieve sustainable profitability.

The cash flow statement tracks the actual movement of capital across operations, investing, and financing activities. Revenue and reported net income mean little if an enterprise cannot convert sales into cash. The dramatic crash of Carvana in 2022 serves as a case study in how growth-at-all-costs models, excessive leverage, and paper inventory assets can collapse when underlying macroeconomic tailwinds suddenly reverse.

Core financial ratios: Diagnosing operational health

Extracting strategic intelligence from financial statements requires analysing key performance metrics across four primary areas: profitability, liquidity, solvency, and operational efficiency.

Profitability ratios such as gross, operating, and net margins, alongside Return on Equity (ROE) and Return on Assets (ROA), measure how efficiently revenues and capital translate into bottom-line profit. Howard Schultz, during his tenure as CEO of Starbucks, consistently focused on maintaining healthy profit margins while expanding the company’s global footprint. This involved careful management of raw material costs, operational efficiencies, and strategic pricing decisions.

Liquidity ratios, including the current and quick ratios, assess an organisation’s capacity to cover short-term obligations using liquid assets. During the early supply chain shocks of 2020, retailers with deep cash reserves navigated severe disruptions, while under-capitalised chains faced sudden operational freezes. Solvency ratios, such as debt-to-equity and debt-to-asset ratios, evaluate long-term stability and reliance on borrowed capital. Efficiency ratios, such as inventory turnover and asset turnover, reveal how effectively company assets and working capital are deployed. Zara founder Amancio Ortega transformed fast fashion by driving exceptionally high inventory turnover, freeing up capital, and reducing markdown risks through tight, real-time supply chain feedback loops.

Capital allocation: Evaluating future investments

A primary responsibility of executive leadership is determining where capital should be deployed. Evaluating strategic growth initiatives, whether internal research and development, physical expansion, or corporate acquisitions, requires a firm grasp of discounted cash flow mechanics.

Net Present Value (NPV) discounts projected cash inflows back to present-day dollars using a risk-adjusted discount rate. A positive NPV demonstrates that an initiative is expected to yield value beyond its risk premium-included capital cost. The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) identifies the break-even discount rate where NPV equals zero. Projects with an IRR exceeding the firm’s hurdle rate usually warrant investment consideration. Meanwhile, the Payback Period measures the time needed to recoup the initial cash outlay. While it ignores the time value of money, it provides a quick assessment of capital recovery risks. During Nvidia’s early development of the CUDA architecture, now beleaguered, Jensen Huang routinely prioritised long-term R&D spending, and parallel computing infrastructure over short-term earnings. Supported by disciplined capital allocation models, these investments built the foundational moat for the company’s ultimate dominance in artificial intelligence computing.

Cost structure and operational discipline

Sustaining profitability requires an understanding of how fixed overhead and variable costs interact under changing market conditions. Fixed costs represent overhead expenses that remain constant regardless of output volume, such as facilities leases and administrative salaries. Variable costs fluctuate directly with production levels, including raw materials, direct labor, and shipping. Identifying the break-even point establishes the precise sales volume needed to cover these combined costs, setting a baseline target for commercial strategy. In mature, capital-intensive sectors, cost control dictates survival. Ceylon Cold Stores (Elephant House) consistently applied this structural discipline in determining pricing of carbonated soft drinks in the face of powerful international and local competition.

Strategic planning, budgeting, and forecasting

Executive decision-making requires looking beyond historic performance to map out future financial trajectories. Financial leadership relies on three foundational processes: budgeting, forecasting, and scenario planning. Budgeting establishes granular resource constraints and financial targets across business units. Forecasting projects future performance using historical operational metrics, market trends, and economic indicators. Scenario modeling builds organisational resilience by mapping out best-case, base-case, and worst-case conditions against potential economic shocks. When Adobe CEO Shantanu Narayen shifted the company’s financial model from perpetual desktop software licenses to a recurring Creative Cloud subscription model, the strategic pivot required long-term financial modeling to manage temporary top-line revenue dips while funding cloud infrastructure, accelerating lifetime customer value.

Risk management and internal oversight

CEOs are responsible for protecting corporate assets and maintaining the integrity of public reporting. This requires monitoring operational, market, and credit risks while establishing strict internal controls to prevent accounting errors or fraudulent activity. The collapse of Wirecard remains a cautionary example of failed governance. Under Markus Braun, aggressive off-balance-sheet misdirection and a total breakdown of internal controls obscured 1.9 billion euros in non-existent cash reserves, leading to complete insolvency and regulatory ruin.

Strategic growth through mergers and acquisitions

Corporate expansion often involves acquiring other market players. Successfully acquiring and integrating target firms requires fluency in valuation, due diligence, and post-merger integration. Valuation involves applying income, market, and asset-based approaches to establish a fair intrinsic price for the target company. Due diligence demands comprehensive audits of the target’s financial ledgers, legal exposures, and operational dependencies. Integration requires merging systems, corporate structures, and workforce cultures post-transaction to capture projected synergies. JKH’s acquisition of Asian Hotels, comprising Cinnamon Grand, Cinnamon Lakeside, Crescat Apartments, and unused freehold land, was a textbook example of acquisition and integration.

When an executive team operates without financial fluency, systemic vulnerabilities multiply rapidly. Strategic capital flows toward low-return initiatives, starving core growth drivers. Ill-considered debt structures expose the enterprise to default during downturns, while inaccurate forecasting damages market credibility and poor oversight invites operational blind spots, fraud, and legal liabilities.

CEOs do not need to handle daily bookkeeping, but they must be capable of auditing the logic behind every financial proposal. Corporate finance fluency transforms quantitative data into a strategic framework, enabling CEOs to ask probing questions of their CFOs, make data-backed operational decisions, and articulate a coherent strategy to shareholders. Ultimately, financial literacy provides the clarity required to navigate economic uncertainty and build enduring enterprise value.

A CEO without financial literacy is akin to Columbus sailing without a compass. He/she may command a magnificent vessel and inspire a brilliant crew yet would be steering blind. In modern business, vision alone cannot navigate the hidden reefs of cash flow crises and volatile markets. Leaving the numbers entirely to the finance team is not delegation; it is surrendering the wheel. True leadership demands reading the financial instruments, interpreting balance sheet currents, and turning hard data into bold strategy.

When a CEO masters the language of finance, the entire dynamic shifts. Uncertainty turns into opportunity. Risk transforms into calculated reward. The fog clears, revealing a sharp, undeniable path to lasting growth. So, step up to the helm. Master your numbers, command your course, and steer your organisation not just toward survival, but toward absolute market dominance. The sky is clear, the ocean is open, and the ultimate destination is yours to claim.

(The author is, currently, a Leadership Coach, Mentor and Consultant and boasts over 50+ years of experience in very senior positions in the Corporate World – local and overseas. www.ronniepeiris.com)

title: Risk of currency fragmentation in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:21
-     - 41

When the United States of America froze the $ 300 billion. Reserve of Russia, it had weaponised and leveraged an instrument which for years textbooks have claimed to be neutral, driven by standards and market efficiency.

Even though still 56.7% of allocated global foreign exchange reserves are accounted as US Dollars, it is observable as per the World Gold Council (WGC), the central bank net purchases hit a record-breaking 289 tons in the second quarter of 2026 alone, which is a dramatic increase in comparison to the number in the Q4 of 2021 which had shown a number of 76.8 tons which outlines a growth approximately of 376%, proving that Central Bank reserve diversification remains actively underway.

Accumulating the trend a prediction has evolved that de-dollarisation is taking effect as BRICS and multiple other bodies and Central Banks move away from the Dollar. However, this de-dollarisation trend has been misread by multiple as an open opportunity to escape liquid availability of the Dollar constraint.

However, that hypothesis has significantly not been accurate about the effect of such fragmentation.

In case of the fragmentation of currency, countries who import a considerable amount of necessary goods such as Sri Lanka would face multiple systemic complications and constraints.

Finance charges would be increased due to Licensed Commercial Banks as profit maximising entities, institutions passing these high, multi-currency volatility risks directly onto businesses through inflated fees, driving up import prices that are ultimately absorbed by the end consumer. During foreign exchange stress cycles (such as 2022-2024), official trade statistics from the Central Bank of Sri Lanka showed that while raw import volumes of key commodities fluctuated, the financial service fees, exchange spreads, and trade credit charges incurred by importers doubled or tripled compared to baseline operational years.

Furthermore, international trade surveys by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) highlight that the global trade finance gap (unmet demand for trade credit) widened to over $ 2.5 trillion, hitting small open economies hardest because regional commercial banks demand higher risk premiums when clearing outside primary dollars.

As Sri Lanka’s domestic manufacturing sector generates roughly 15% to 20% of GDP, heavily concentrated in light manufacturing (apparel, rubber products, tea processing as confirmed by the Department of Census and Statistics (DCS), National Accounts Estimates of Sri Lanka. And if Sri Lanka ever relies heavily on critical imports from a trade partner operating outside the centralised Dollar network, any localised currency deficit or clearing failure within that fragmented bilateral corridor directly threatens the broader economy. Deprived of the deep, volatility absorbing liquidity buffer provided by global dollar rails, small open economies face immediate settlement bottlenecks. Forcing a sudden pivot toward domestic import substitution under such strain is an operational nightmare; domestic production capacity cannot rapidly scale to replace multi-billion-dollar global supply chains.

Under modern nuclear deterrence, ‘great power’ friction shifts into proxy conflicts and supply-chain disruptions, which is an issue even the deterrence factor that has controlled modern conflict so far wouldn’t  be able to control. Viewed through a geo-economic lens, research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Geoeconomic Fragmentation, there is a direct mathematical link between “geopolitical distance” (divergence in UN voting records) and cross-border financial flows.

For Sri Lankan corporate treasurers and commercial banks, this means moving away from passive exposure to bilateral currency shifts. Businesses must actively hedge against emerging clearing bottlenecks rather than treating alternative trade corridors as a frictionless silver bullet.

Ultimately, global monetary fragmentation acts as a hidden tax on Sri Lanka’s economy. Without smooth dollar-clearing channels, essential imports become pricier and our foreign debt obligations grow even more dangerous and threatening. Navigating such a fractured financial landscape will require clearheaded realism from policymakers building strong reserve buffers and managing risk long before the next global shock hits our shores.

This analysis is compiled from independent research into macro-financial trends, utilising data from the World Gold Council, the Asian Development Bank, the IMF, and the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, and was solely compiled and articulated.

title: Economic outlook takes centre stage at EY post-Budget forum | Daily FT

Ernst & Young (EY) Sri Lanka successfully marked another edition of its annual Post-Budget Forum last week, at Cinnamon Life at City of Dreams. The event brought together senior Government officials, policymakers and business leaders from across the country to examine the key highlights of the National Budget 2027 and the opportunities and considerations they present for Sri Lanka’s economy and businesses.

The forum commenced with a welcome address by EY Sri Lanka and Maldives Country Managing Partner Gayathri Manatunga, who welcomed the distinguished guests and set the stage for the evening’s discussions on the National Budget 2027 and its implications for Sri Lanka’s economic landscape.

The program featured insights from EY Sri Lanka and Maldives Partner and Head of Tax Sulaiman Nishtar, who delivered a comprehensive presentation on the key tax proposals and fiscal measures outlined in the National Budget 2027.

His presentation covered areas including the growth agenda and priority sectors, investment and capital formation, tax policies and tax administration, and the cost of doing business, providing participants with an overview of the potential implications for businesses and the wider economy.

The presentation was followed by a panel discussion moderated by Nishtar, bringing together Secretary to the Treasury Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma, Senior Economic Adviser to the President and Board of Investment of Sri Lanka Chairman Duminda Hulangamuwa, Sri Lanka Ports Authority Chairman Dr. Parakrama Dissanayake, Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Chairman Krishan Balendra and Ernst & Young Sri Lanka Partner Tax Shehani Paranavitane.

The discussion explored the broader economic direction outlined in the Budget, with particular attention to fiscal priorities, economic resilience, investment opportunities and the implications of policy measures for Sri Lankan businesses. Dr. Suriyapperuma shared perspectives on the Government’s fiscal direction and the economic considerations underpinning the Budget, contributing to a broader discussion on the country’s economic priorities and the way forward.

The evening concluded with a cocktail reception, creating an opportunity for participants to extend the conversation and exchange perspectives with leaders from the public and private sectors.

A fixture on Sri Lanka’s corporate calendar for over a decade, the EY Sri Lanka Post-Budget Forum continues to advance public-private dialogue and provide businesses with timely insights into the country’s fiscal and economic direction.

title: Sri Lanka fight back but Pakistan sniff victory | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:06

Lead by 82 with a wicket in hand

RAWALPINDI: Sri Lanka fought hard on day three of the second Test to deny Pakistan victory inside three days at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium yesterday, ending the day on 309-9 to hold onto an overall lead of 82 with only one wicket and two days of the match remaining.

As it stand it is Pakistan’s Test and series to lose.      

Starting the day at 74-3, Sri Lanka lost Dhananjaya de Silva and Pasindu Sooriyabandara the two overnight batsmen in the first session and it looked like they would fold up quickly. But skipper Kusal Mendis, Sonal Dinusha and Milan Rathnayaka all fought hard with each making a fifty.

Mendis and Dinusha were dismissed shortly after the milestone – Mendis for 53 (126 balls, 8 fours) in an unlucky fashion, dragging a loose delivery down leg onto his own stumps, and Dinusha for 54 (119 balls, 7 fours) to bring to an end an 81-run partnership. Rathnayaka stood tall though -60* off 82 balls (11 fours) and he is the key if Sri Lanka are to extend the lead beyond 100.

This is only the third time Sri Lanka’s No. 6-8 batters have all scored 50+ in the same Test innings, after doing so against Zimbabwe in 2001 and Bangladesh in 2007, both at the SSC.

While Sri Lanka can be proud of the way they have battled yesterday, they’ll be rankled with some of the soft dismissals, which robbed them of gaining an even bigger lead.

Pakistan toiled hard in the absence of Saqib Khan (left hamstring injury). Aamer Jamal took three wickets and Mohammad Abbas chipped in with two.

Pakistan will look forward to taking the last wicket early today and then chasing down the target without any alarms.

title: SLC clarifies reports on ICC men’s event hosting allocations | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:05
-     - 12

Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) yesterday clarified the position regarding recent media reports suggesting that Sri Lanka will not host any major ICC men’s cricket tournament through 2035.

The ICC announced the hosting allocations for its men’s white-ball events covering the period from 2024 to 2031 on 16 November 2021. Accordingly, Sri Lanka successfully co-hosted the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup 2026 with India as part of those allocations.

The same announcement identified India as the host of the 2029 ICC Men’s Champions Trophy and India and Bangladesh as joint hosts of the 2031 ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup. These hosting arrangements were therefore announced in 2021 and are not new allocations arising from the recent ICC meetings in Bali.

The ICC’s latest announcement, dated 15 November, confirms the tournament calendar and event windows through 2035. However, the host countries for the men’s events scheduled from 2032 to 2035 remain unconfirmed.

Accordingly, the latest announcement does not in any way say that Sri Lanka has been ruled out of hosting ICC men’s cricket events through 2035. The confirmation of tournament dates should not be interpreted as the completion of hosting allocations for that period.

title: Final chance for bottom ranked teams to avoid relegation | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:04
-     - 14

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

For teams that are at the bottom of the pile BRC (1.85 weightage points), Nugegoda SWC (1.84), Badureliya CC (1.58) and Kurunegala YCC (0.62) the Major Club 4-day league which commenced yesterday will be of great importance.

As per the directive issued by the SLC Transformation Committee the three teams that finish at the bottom of the rankings at the completion of the three Major Club tournaments – T20, 50-over and 4-day will be relegated to Tier B. So it is imperative that the four clubs from the bottom improve their performances in the Major Club 4-day League, lest they finish in the bottom three and get relegated.

The Major T20 and 50-over tournaments have already been completed and at the end of it, SSC has emerged as the top ranked team amongst the 14 clubs participating. SSC finished runner-up in both the T20 and 50-over tournaments and have garnered 6.37 weightage points. They are followed by CCC (5.64) and Moors SC (5.54). Moors SC won the 50-over final and Tamil Union the T20 final.

Nugegoda SWC have begun their fight to avoid relegation in emphatic fashion by thumping a depleted NCC bowling attack to the tune of 383-4 at the Mahinda Rajapaksa Stadium, Hambantota. Centuries from Lohan de Zoysa (144 off 188 balls, 16 fours, 1 six) and Akram Muthalib (136 off 182 balls, 12 fours, 2 sixes) and their partnership of 261 for the second wicket laid the foundation for Nugegoda SWC’s big total. Kevin Perera also joined the party scoring a solid 63 off 107 balls (3 fours, 1 six).

Badureliya CC, another team fighting against relegation did not have things easy at the Galle Stadium where Police SC rattled off 332-2. Tillakaratne Sampath, brother of former Sri Lanka captain Tillakaratne Dilshan hit a career best 169* at the age of 44 to steer Police SC to the total. Sampath hit 19 fours and a six in his 279-ball knock and figured in a 216 with Dulash Udayanga who missed out on a century by two runs (98 off 225 balls, 13 fours).

In the fight against relegation BRC held the upper hand at the end of day one against Kurunegala YCC at the R Premadasa Stadium. A 126 runs stand for the fifth wicket between Promod Maduwantha (58 off 164 balls, 7 fours) and Raminda Wijesooriya (85* off 146 balls, 7 fours, 3 sixes) saw BRC end the tedious day at 256-5. Skipper Hashan Dumindu scored 52 off 95 balls (9 fours) at the top.

Spinners Ramesh Mendis (4/65) and Duvindu Tillakaratne (3/47) bundled out SSC for 244 at the NCC grounds. After losing their first two wickets for one run to Santhush Gunathilake, it was a hard struggle for SSC to come up with a competitive total. Dasun Shanaka played an unusual innings of 41 off 64 balls (3 fours) and Malsha Fernando made 71 off 79 balls (7 fours, 2 sixes) for SSC to recover from 91-5 to their final total. Moors SC were 28 without loss by the close.

CCC powered their way to a first innings lead over Tamil Union at the Pallekele Stadium. Tamil Union succumbed to 179 against the left-arm seam and spin of Vishwa Fernando (3/50) and Dilum Sudeera (4/39). Navod Paranavithana and skipper Minod Bhanuka made 40s apiece in a partnership of 93. CCC openers made light of Tamil Union’s total by posting 188 for the first wicket. Sarith Sudeena, 19-year-old diminutive left-hander from De Mazenod College, Kandana made a memorable beginning to his first-class career scoring an attractive 110 off 91 balls (17 fours, 2 sixes). Another 19-year-old Dulnith Sigera of Mahanama College was unbeaten on 77 (102 balls, 6 fours, 3 sixes) – four short of equaling his career best score.

Lahiru Madushanka played a captain’s innings of 119* off 198 balls (11 fours, 1 six) to lift Bloomfield from a precarious 36-4 to a respectable 283-6 against Panadura SC at the Rangiri Dambulla Stadium. Kasun Abeyratne led the revival with a fighting knock of 80 off 122 balls (8 fours) after which Madushanka and Shanikya Deshapriya (40) put on 90 to continue the recovery.

All the matches will continue on the second day today.

No other Sri Lankan batter comes close to these figures. Hasini Perera is the only other player to score a half-century. Other than that the Sri Lankan middle order has not contributed so much.

Sri Lanka will be hoping that Vishmi will be able to continue with her form in the Super Six stage as well because the middle order has not been able to deliver in the four matches played so far. Vishmi has more or less been carrying the batting on her shoulders.   

Sri Lanka’s main concern is the lack of form shown by their captain Harshitha Samarawickrama. The three innings she has played has produced only 36 runs with a top score of 24. If she comes good the lack of runs in Sri Lanka’s middle order will be solved to a great extent.

In the bowling it has been their spinners who have been proactive with Kavisha Dilhari (8 wickets), Sugandika Kumari (5) and Nimasha Meepage (4) among the main wicket-takers and seamer Sathya Sandeepani (7) providing the initial breakthrough.

Zimbabwe’s 17-year-old left-arm seamer Christine Mutasa is the leading wicket-taker in the tournament with 11 wickets at an economy rate of 4.85 while left-hand batting all-rounder Kelis Ndhlovu has been their leading run scorer with 166 runs (avg. 41.50) inclusive of two fifties. (ST)

title: Kalyani’s five-for sets up South Asia’s win | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:00

Kalyani took five wickets to set up South Asia’s six-wicket victory over Australasia in the inaugural Test Twenty tournament at the SSC yesterday.

It was the second win of the tournament for Rajkumar Sharma’s side, who took a 78-run lead through their girls’ XI before Harshit Tiwari struck 45 off 24 balls to finish the job against Matthew Hayden’s Australasia.

In Test Twenty, the girls’ and boys’ XIs each bat for up to 20 overs, with their scores combined to decide the match. South Asia’s girls restricted Australasia to 102-8 and replied with 180-5, leaving their boys a target of 110 after Australasia posted 187-8.

Kalyani took 5/19 from four overs, bowling 12 dot balls. Bhakti Shetty top-scored with 18 for Australasia, while Varsha Yadav made 17.

Siya Chugh anchored South Asia’s reply with an unbeaten 41 off 40 balls. Suhani Bharatkumar Kahandal supplied the acceleration, hitting seven fours in her 35 off 20, and Aadhya Sah added 27 off 17. Sophie Louise Warrilow took two wickets.

Divyansh Chauhan led Australasia’s fight back with 50 off 32 balls. Anurag Yadav struck 43 off 23, Ibrahim Khan made 35 off 20 and Vansh Gemini hit four sixes in his 31 off 17. Aditya Bhatt checked their progress with 4/18, while Tiwari took 2/27. Kalyani and Bhatt shared the Player of the Match award.

Tiwari then led the chase and Sai Gopal Rathod chipped in with 20 off 10 balls as South Asia reached 110-4 in 14.2 overs. Rayyan Hussain and Chirag Singla took two wickets apiece for Australasia.
